subsection: 3. Exchanges of water between oceans and atmosphere

notes.b: Water is constantly moving between the oceans, the air and the land. This continuous circulation is the hydrological (water) cycle, and it is the starting point for understanding how the oceans and atmosphere exchange water.
points: The cycle is a closed system, meaning nothing enters or leaves: the total amount of water on earth stays the same, and water only moves between stores (the places where it is held).

Two forces drive the movement: solar energy, which powers evaporation (liquid water turning to vapour), and gravity, which pulls water down as precipitation (rain, snow and so on) and runoff (water flowing over the land).
Diagram: draw a labelled cycle from ocean to atmosphere to land and back, with the stores drawn as boxes and the flows as arrows.
notes.tip: Exams ask about the hydrological cycle and its ocean-atmosphere exchanges, so a labelled diagram with stores as boxes and flows as arrows is worth drawing.

notes.b: A store is a place where water is held for a time. The oceans dwarf all the others, and only a tiny part of the earth's water is fresh liquid water at the surface.
points: Oceans hold about 97% of the earth's water; ice sheets and glaciers hold about 2%, most of it in Antarctica; groundwater (water stored underground in soil and rock) holds under 1%.
Lakes, rivers, soil moisture, the atmosphere and living things together hold only a tiny fraction. The atmosphere holds about 0.001% of the earth's water.
About 2.5-3% of all water is fresh (not salty), and most of that is frozen, so liquid fresh surface water is a very small part of the total.

notes.b: Flows are the processes that move water from one store to another. Each has its own name, and the ocean-atmosphere exchange depends on the first few.
points: Evaporation: liquid water turns to vapour (water as an invisible gas), mainly from the ocean because the oceans are by far the biggest store.
Transpiration: vapour is released from plant leaves; evapotranspiration is transpiration and evaporation combined over land.
Sublimation: ice turns directly into vapour without first melting.
Advection: wind carries water vapour horizontally from sea to land, so rain can fall far from where the water evaporated.
Condensation: vapour turns to liquid droplets, forming cloud, fog or dew, for example when air cools.

Precipitation, interception (rain caught by leaves), infiltration (soaking into the soil), surface runoff, throughflow (water moving sideways through soil) and groundwater flow return water to the sea. There is more on these drainage-basin flows in the chapter Rivers - Fluvial Processes and Landforms.

notes.b: The oceans are both the main source and the main destination of the water that moves through the air. This shows how much of the cycle happens over the sea.
points: Roughly 85-90% of global evaporation comes from the oceans, and roughly three-quarters of global precipitation falls on them.
Evaporation over the oceans exceeds the rain falling back on them, so the surplus is carried over the land by wind, and returns to the sea through rivers and groundwater.
notes.tip: Give only these rounded shares when describing the exchange: most evaporation is from the oceans and most precipitation falls back on them.

notes.b: Residence time is how long a water molecule stays in a store before moving on. It differs enormously between stores.
points: Water stays in the atmosphere for only about 9 days on average, but in the ocean for thousands of years and in the Antarctic ice sheet for far longer.
The atmosphere's water is therefore recycled quickly, while ocean water changes slowly.

notes.b: The exchange is not the same everywhere. Where evaporation and precipitation differ, distinctive climates result, and human activity can change the balance.
points: Evaporation exceeds precipitation over the subtropical oceans, which helps explain their high salinity (saltiness), because water leaves but the salt stays. There is more on this in The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems.
Precipitation exceeds evaporation in the equatorial belt and in the mid-latitude westerly belt (the zone of prevailing westerly winds).
Deforestation reduces evapotranspiration and so the recycling of rainfall; a large share of the Amazon's rain is water recycled from the forest by evapotranspiration.
Global warming intensifies the water cycle. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
notes.tip: For the Amazon, link deforestation to less evapotranspiration and so less rainfall recycling.

notes.b: Humidity describes how much water vapour the air holds. It matters because it decides whether air can form cloud, fog or dew.
points: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour in a volume of air, in g/m³.
Relative humidity is the amount of water vapour present as a percentage of the most the air could hold at that temperature. Saturated air (air holding all it can) has a relative humidity of 100%.
Warm air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each 1 °C rise in temperature, so warm air holds much more than cold air.

Cooling air raises its relative humidity without adding any water, because the most it can hold falls; warming lowers it. This is why relative humidity is usually highest at dawn and lowest in mid-afternoon.
Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated as it cools; further cooling causes condensation. There is more on measuring humidity in The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems.
notes.tip: Relative humidity is a percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature, not the amount of water in the air; that is absolute humidity. Remember that cooling raises relative humidity without adding any water.

notes.b: The amount of vapour in the air affects how evaporation works, and so how the climate feels and how temperatures behave.
points: High humidity in the tropics makes heat oppressive, because sweat evaporates slowly into air that is already full of vapour.
Low humidity in deserts allows rapid evaporation and large daily temperature ranges (the difference between day and night temperature).

notes.b: Evaporation is the step that puts water into the atmosphere. Its rate depends on energy, on the state of the air and on whether there is water to evaporate.
points: Evaporation is water molecules gaining enough energy to escape as vapour. It takes latent heat (hidden heat energy) from the surface, cooling it, and that energy is released again on condensation. There is more on this in Solar energy and its redistribution.
Higher temperature increases evaporation because it gives more energy; strong sunshine and low air pressure also increase it.
Drier air, with low relative humidity, increases evaporation because it can take up more vapour.
Wind increases evaporation by removing moist air and replacing it with drier air.
A large supply of water, such as oceans, lakes or wet ground, allows evaporation to continue.

notes.b: Because evaporation needs heat, wind and water together, it is strongest in some parts of the world and weak in others.
points: Evaporation is greatest over the subtropical oceans under clear skies and steady trade winds (the regular winds blowing towards the equator), and along warm currents such as the Gulf Stream; it is least over cold polar seas.

Potential evapotranspiration (the water that could evaporate if supply were unlimited) far exceeds rainfall in hot deserts, which is the cause of drought. There is more on this in Climate and economic development.

notes.b: Condensation is the reverse of evaporation and is how clouds begin. Vapour will not simply turn to droplets in clean air, so it needs something to form on.
points: Condensation is water vapour turning into liquid droplets when air cools to its dew point (the temperature at which it is saturated).
Condensation needs condensation nuclei: tiny particles of dust, sea salt, smoke or pollen around which droplets form.

notes.h: How air is cooled to dew point
notes.b: Air only condenses when it is cooled to dew point, so the question is what cools it. There are four ways.
points: Adiabatic cooling (cooling caused by expansion, with no heat lost) of rising air is the main cause of cloud.
Contact cooling by radiation occurs when air touches ground that has lost heat at night.
Advection cooling occurs when warm, moist air moves over a cold surface.
Mixing of air masses of different temperatures can bring air to dew point, because the blend is cooler than the warm air alone.

notes.b: Rising air cools even though no heat is taken from it. Understanding why explains cloud height and the rates at which air cools.
points: Rising air expands because pressure falls with height, and it cools without losing heat to its surroundings; sinking air is compressed and warms.
Unsaturated air cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate (the rate of cooling with height), about 10 °C per 1,000 m.
Once condensation begins, the latent heat released slows the cooling to the saturated adiabatic lapse rate, about 5-7 °C per 1,000 m, which varies with temperature.
The height at which condensation begins is the condensation level, or cloud base.
notes.tip: Rising air cools because it expands, not because it is higher and closer to space or because it meets cold air.

notes.b: Whether rising air keeps rising depends on how its temperature compares with the air around it. This decides whether the sky gives towering storm cloud or flat layer cloud.
points: Unstable air: if rising air stays warmer than its surroundings, because the environment cools faster than the rising air does, it keeps rising and forms towering cumulus, showers and thunderstorms. The environmental lapse rate (the cooling of the surrounding air with height) averages about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.
Stable air: if rising air becomes cooler than its surroundings, it sinks back, giving layer cloud or clear skies.
A temperature inversion, with warmer air above cooler air, is very stable because the cooler air below cannot rise, and it traps fog and pollution.
Diagram: a temperature-height graph comparing the environmental and adiabatic lapse rates.

notes.b: Condensation also happens at ground level, where it gives dew, frost and fog. The type depends on how the air is cooled.
points: Dew forms on surfaces cooled below dew point on clear, calm nights.
Hoar frost forms when the dew point is below 0 °C, as vapour turns straight to ice crystals.
Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights, usually under anticyclones (areas of high pressure) in autumn and winter, in valleys and hollows; it burns off in the morning sun.

Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves over a cold sea or land. The Grand Banks off Newfoundland, Canada, are among the foggiest places on earth, where warm moist air from over the Gulf Stream crosses the cold Labrador Current.
San Francisco's summer fogs are also advection fog: they form where moist Pacific air crosses the cold California Current.
Hill fog is cloud on high ground, where air is forced up and cools; smog is fog mixed with smoke.
notes.tip: Radiation fog needs clear, calm nights: cloud would stop the ground losing heat and wind would mix the air. Advection fog can form in wind.

notes.b: Clouds form wherever air is lifted and cooled below its dew point. The ways air is forced upward give five causes of cloud.
points: Clouds are visible masses of tiny water droplets or ice crystals, formed when rising air cools below its dew point.
Convection: uplift from surface heating, which warms the air so that it rises.
Orographic (relief) uplift: air is forced up over high ground.
Frontal uplift: warm air rises over cold air at a front (the boundary between two air masses).
Convergence: air streams meet and, with nowhere else to go, are forced upward, as at the ITCZ (the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds meet).
Turbulence: mixing of air that lifts it.

notes.b: Cloud names are built from a few Latin words that describe shape, height and rain. Once you know them, a name tells you what the cloud looks like and what weather it brings.
points: Luke Howard, an English pharmacist and amateur meteorologist, proposed the Latin cloud names cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus in 1803.
Cirrus means wispy and fibrous, a curl of hair; cumulus means heaped and puffy, a heap; stratus means a layered sheet.
Nimbus or nimbo- means rain-bearing; alto- means middle level.
The WMO's International Cloud Atlas sets out the ten main cloud types (the WMO is the World Meteorological Organization).

notes.h: High clouds (above about 6,000 m, ice crystals)
notes.b: High clouds sit above about 6,000 m and are made of ice crystals. All three types here are thin, wispy or veil-like clouds.
points: Cirrus: thin wisps, often called mares' tails; fair weather, but often the first sign of an approaching warm front.
Cirrostratus: a thin milky veil that produces a halo round the sun or moon; rain is likely within hours.
Cirrocumulus: small ripples, known as a mackerel sky because the pattern looks like fish scales.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the ten cloud types by height with their weather. Heights are approximate for mid-latitudes.

notes.b: Middle clouds sit between about 2,000 m and 6,000 m, which is why their names begin with alto-, meaning middle level.
points: Altocumulus: grey or white patches in rolls.
Altostratus: a grey sheet through which the sun shows as if through frosted glass; it thickens ahead of a warm front.

notes.b: Low clouds are the ones that most often sit over Ireland and bring its drizzle and steady rain.
points: Stratus: a grey, featureless layer, so it has no towering shape, that produces drizzle and hill fog.
Stratocumulus: a lumpy grey layer, the commonest cloud over Ireland, usually dry or giving light drizzle.
Nimbostratus: a thick, dark rain cloud giving long periods of steady rain or snow at warm fronts.
notes.tip: Nimbostratus gives steady frontal rain and stratus gives drizzle. Thunder and hail come from cumulonimbus, not nimbostratus.

notes.b: Some clouds do not stay in one layer. Their base is low but their tops reach high, because strong rising air builds them upward.
points: Cumulus: fair-weather heaps with flat bases on sunny days, which can grow into showers if the air keeps rising.

Cumulonimbus: a towering cloud with an anvil-shaped top spreading at the tropopause (the top of the lowest layer of the atmosphere), bringing heavy showers, hail, thunder and lightning, and squalls (sudden strong gusts).
Heights are approximate for mid-latitudes.
notes.tip: Cumulonimbus, not nimbostratus, gives thunder and hail.

notes.b: Clouds appear in a predictable order as a front approaches, so they can be used to forecast weather.
points: Ahead of a warm front, cirrus is followed by cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus in turn. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Cumulonimbus marks a cold front.
Diagram: a chart of the ten cloud types arranged by height.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the ten types by height with their weather, so practise the height chart.

notes.b: Clouds affect temperature on the ground as well as producing rain, and the effect depends on the type of cloud.
points: Low thick clouds cool the surface by reflecting sunlight; high thin clouds warm it by trapping long-wave radiation (heat given off by the earth); cloudy nights are milder.

notes.b: Cloud is not the same as rain. Droplets must first grow, by one of two processes, before they can fall.
points: Cloud droplets are far too small to fall; they must grow about a million times in volume to form a raindrop heavy enough to reach the ground.

notes.b: In cold clouds, ice crystals grow at the expense of water droplets. This is the main way rain forms in Ireland.
points: In clouds colder than 0 °C, supercooled droplets (liquid droplets still unfrozen below 0 °C) and ice crystals exist together. Vapour is deposited on the ice crystals, which grow at the droplets' expense, become heavy and fall as snow, melting into rain below the freezing level.
This Bergeron-Findeisen process is the main one in mid-latitude clouds, including Ireland's.
notes.tip: Name this process the Bergeron-Findeisen process and explain it, rather than calling it just the Bergeron process.

notes.b: In clouds that are never cold enough for ice, droplets grow by colliding with each other instead.
points: In warm clouds, which are above 0 °C throughout and are common in the tropics, larger droplets fall faster, collide with and absorb smaller ones (coalesce) until they are heavy enough to fall.

notes.b: Precipitation can fall as liquid or ice. The form depends on the size of the drops and on the temperature of the air they fall through.
points: Rain: liquid drops, such as the steady rain from nimbostratus.
Drizzle: very small drops falling from stratus.
Snow: ice crystals clumped as flakes, falling when the air is near or below freezing to the ground.
Sleet: melting snow, or rain and snow mixed.
Hail: layered ice balls formed when strong updrafts in cumulonimbus carry frozen drops up and down repeatedly, adding layers until they are too heavy; hail is mostly a warm-season phenomenon.
Freezing rain and glaze: rain that freezes on contact with cold surfaces.
notes.tip: Hail forms in strong updrafts inside cumulonimbus, mostly in warm seasons. It is not frozen rain; that is sleet or ice pellets.

notes.b: Convectional rain comes from air that is heated from below and rises. It is the daily rain of the equator.
points: 1. The ground is heated strongly, warming the air above it.
2. The warm air expands, rises and cools adiabatically.
3. When it reaches dew point, cumulus and then cumulonimbus clouds form.
4. Heavy showers, often with thunder, follow, usually in the afternoon, because that is when the ground is hottest.
This type is typical of the equatorial belt every day, and of Irish summer afternoons occasionally, especially inland.
Diagram: a column of rising air above heated ground, topped by cumulonimbus.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the three types of rainfall, so learn each as numbered stages with a diagram.

notes.b: Relief rain forms when moist air is forced up over mountains. It leaves a wet windward side and a dry leeward side.
points: 1. Moist air from the sea is forced to rise over a mountain barrier.
2. It cools, condenses and gives heavy rain on the windward slope (the side facing the wind).
3. On the leeward side (the sheltered side) the air descends, is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate and a rain shadow (a dry area) results.
4. A warm, dry föhn-type wind may blow down the lee side. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Ireland's west coast mountains receive this rain.

In India, the Western Ghats force the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise, giving heavy rain on the Konkan and Malabar coasts, with the Deccan in rain shadow; Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in the Khasi Hills, Meghalaya, are among the wettest places on earth.
Diagram: a cross-section of a mountain barrier showing the windward wet slope and the leeward rain shadow.
notes.tip: The leeward side gets less rain because the descending air warms, not just because the rain has all fallen. Don't give rainfall totals for Mawsynram or Cherrapunji.

notes.b: Frontal rain falls where warm air meets cold air in a depression (a low-pressure weather system). It is Ireland's main source of rain.
points: 1. In a depression, warm, moist tropical air is forced to rise over cold polar air at the warm front, giving gentle ascent and long, steady rain.
2. At the cold front the warm air is undercut, causing sharp ascent and short, heavy showers.
Frontal rain is Ireland's main source of rain. There is more on depressions in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.

notes.b: Rain also falls where winds meet, because air that cannot go sideways is forced upward.
points: Where air streams meet they are forced to rise, as where the trade winds converge at the ITCZ, giving heavy rain.

notes.b: World rainfall follows the pressure belts, which are bands of rising or sinking air arranged by latitude. Rising air gives rain and sinking air gives dry conditions.
points: Equatorial belt (about 0-10°): heavy rain all year, over 2,000 mm a year, from low pressure, rising air, convergence at the ITCZ, convection and high evaporation from warm seas and forests. Manaus, central Amazon, Brazil, receives about 2,300 mm a year.
Tropics with a wet and dry season (about 10-20°, savanna and monsoon lands): rain falls in summer when the ITCZ moves over them, and the winter is dry.
Subtropical high-pressure belts (about 20-30°): very low rainfall and the world's great hot deserts, from sinking, warming, stable air and clear skies.
The Atacama, Chile, is the driest non-polar desert on earth, and the Namib receives much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current.
Mid-latitudes (about 40-60°): moderate to heavy rain from depressions in the westerlies, wettest on west coasts facing onshore winds (Ireland), decreasing into continental interiors.
Polar regions: very low precipitation, since cold air holds little vapour and sinking air lies under the polar high pressure. Antarctica is the driest continent, a cold desert.
Diagram: a pole-to-pole profile of rainfall under the three-cell model (the pattern of three circulation cells in each hemisphere).
notes.tip: Explain each rainfall zone by its pressure belt, and name regions. Exams ask for the global distribution of precipitation by pressure belt with modifying factors.

notes.b: The latitude pattern is changed locally by five factors, each of which can make a place wetter or drier than its latitude suggests.
points: Relief and rain shadow: the leeward side of a mountain barrier receives much less rain. There is more on this in the block on relief (orographic) rainfall.
Distance from the sea: continental interiors are dry because they lie far from the moisture of the oceans.
Prevailing winds: onshore winds bring rain, while offshore winds bring dry air.
Ocean currents: warm currents add moisture and instability; cold currents chill the air and make it stable, so rain is rare though fog is common on the coasts named above.
Seasonal migration: the pressure belts move north and south with the overhead sun, shifting the rain belts with them.

notes.b: A rainfall regime is the pattern of rain through the year. Five regimes are worth knowing.
points: Equatorial: rain all year because the air is warm and rising every day, often peaking after the equinoxes.
Monsoon: a very wet summer and a dry winter, as in India.
Mediterranean: a wet winter and a dry summer.
Continental interiors: a summer maximum, because summer heating drives convection.
Irish (oceanic): rain all year, with a maximum in autumn and winter.

notes.b: Ireland shows how wind, depressions and relief combine to make the west wet and the east drier.
points: The west is wetter than the east, the mountains are wettest, and the west has more wet days, because moist Atlantic air arrives there first.
Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin, about 1,000-1,250 mm across much of the west, and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains.
Wet days number about 150 a year on the east and south-east coasts, and up to about 225 a year in parts of the west.
Causes: prevailing south-westerly winds, Atlantic depressions reaching the west first, relief uplift on the western mountains, and the rain shadow in the east.

notes.b: Variability is how much rainfall changes from year to year. It is a problem for farming and water supply.
points: Rainfall is least reliable where totals are lowest. In the Sahel, annual rainfall is roughly 200-600 mm, falling in one short summer wet season when the ITCZ moves north.
It varies greatly from year to year, so drought risk is greatest there. There is more on this in One major biome in detail.

notes.b: The exchanges of water between ocean and atmosphere give rise to distinctive weather and climate regimes in different parts of the world. Each is a one-line summary here.
points: Equatorial regime: morning heating gives way to afternoon storms every day.
Monsoon regime: moist sea air brings a wet summer and dry land air a dry winter over India, as the monsoon (a seasonal wind) reverses.
Fog deserts: cold-current coasts, such as the Atacama and Namib, have fog rather than rain.
Irish maritime regime: a cool, cloudy, wet climate fed by moisture from the Atlantic and warmed by the North Atlantic Drift.
Snowy continental and lake-effect winters: cold, snowy winters with heavy snowfall downwind of large lakes and in continental interiors.
Intensified water cycle: warming increases evaporation and brings heavier downpours. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
notes.tip: For regime questions, give the processes first, then name regimes (equatorial, monsoon, desert, Mediterranean, Irish oceanic) and tie each to the exchange of water.

keyTerms.definition: The continuous movement of water between the oceans, atmosphere, land and living things, driven by solar energy and gravity.
The average time a water molecule stays in one store, such as the atmosphere or the ocean.
The amount of water vapour in the air as a percentage of the most it could hold at that temperature.
The temperature to which air must cool for it to become saturated and for condensation to begin.
Tiny airborne particles, such as dust, sea salt or smoke, around which water droplets form.
The cooling of rising air as it expands in lower pressure, without losing heat to its surroundings.
The height at which rising air cools to dew point and cloud begins to form.
The growth of ice crystals at the expense of supercooled droplets in clouds colder than 0 °C, leading to snowfall.
The process in warm clouds in which larger droplets collide with and absorb smaller ones until they fall as rain.
The dry leeward side of a mountain barrier, where descending air warms and clouds evaporate.
Rain produced when strongly heated ground warms the air above it, which rises, cools and forms cumulonimbus clouds.
Fog formed when warm, moist air moves over a colder surface, such as a cold sea.

factCards.term: Hydrological cycle: share of the earth's water in each main store
factCards.definition: Oceans about 97%; ice sheets and glaciers about 2%, most of it in Antarctica; groundwater under 1%; the atmosphere only about 0.001%. Only about 2.5–3% of all water is fresh, and most of that is frozen.

factCards.term: Ocean–atmosphere water exchange: key shares and residence time
factCards.definition: About 85–90% of evaporation is from the oceans and about three-quarters of precipitation falls on them; wind carries the surplus over land and rivers return it. Vapour stays about 9 days in the atmosphere, but water stays thousands of years in the ocean.

factCards.term: Why relative humidity is usually highest at dawn and lowest in mid-afternoon
factCards.definition: Warm air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each 1 °C rise. Cooling air raises its relative humidity without adding water and warming lowers it, so humidity peaks in the cool of dawn and falls in the afternoon heat.

factCards.term: Evaporation: five factors that increase its rate
factCards.definition: Higher temperature and strong sunshine (more energy); dry air with low relative humidity; wind, which replaces moist air with drier air; a large supply of water such as oceans, lakes or wet ground; low air pressure.

factCards.term: Four ways air is cooled to its dew point
factCards.definition: Adiabatic cooling of rising air, the main cause of cloud; contact cooling when air touches ground that has lost heat at night; advection cooling when warm, moist air moves over a cold surface; mixing of air masses of different temperature.

factCards.term: Adiabatic lapse rates: the dry, saturated and environmental figures
factCards.definition: Unsaturated rising air cools at the dry adiabatic rate, about 10 °C per 1,000 m; once condensation begins, released latent heat slows cooling to the saturated rate, about 5–7 °C per 1,000 m. The environmental lapse rate averages about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.

factCards.term: Stable and unstable air: what happens and the weather each gives
factCards.definition: Unstable: rising air stays warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising, giving towering cumulus, showers and thunderstorms. Stable: rising air turns cooler than its surroundings and sinks back, giving layer cloud or clear skies. An inversion traps fog.

factCards.term: Radiation fog: conditions and how it forms
factCards.definition: On clear, calm nights, usually under anticyclones in autumn and winter, the ground loses heat and cools the air touching it to dew point; fog gathers in valleys and hollows and burns off in the morning sun. Cloud or wind would prevent it.

factCards.term: Advection fog: two named examples and why they form
factCards.definition: The Grand Banks off Newfoundland, Canada, among the foggiest places on earth, where warm moist air from over the Gulf Stream crosses the cold Labrador Current; San Francisco's summer fogs, where moist Pacific air crosses the cold California Current.

factCards.term: Cloud names: who devised them and what the Latin words mean
factCards.definition: Luke Howard, an English pharmacist and amateur meteorologist, in 1803: cirrus (wispy, a curl of hair), cumulus (a heap), stratus (a layer), nimbus (rain-bearing). Alto- means middle level. The WMO sets ten main cloud types.

factCards.term: High clouds: three types with their appearance and weather
factCards.definition: Above about 6,000 m, of ice crystals: cirrus (wisps, mares' tails; fair, but may herald a warm front); cirrostratus (a milky veil with a halo round the sun or moon; rain likely within hours); cirrocumulus (small ripples, a mackerel sky).

factCards.term: Middle and low clouds: five types, their appearance and weather
factCards.definition: Altocumulus (patches in rolls); altostratus (sun as if through frosted glass, thickening ahead of a warm front); stratus (drizzle, hill fog); stratocumulus (commonest over Ireland, dry or light drizzle); nimbostratus (long, steady rain or snow at warm fronts).

factCards.term: Cumulonimbus: appearance, weather and how hail forms in it
factCards.definition: A towering cloud with an anvil top spreading at the tropopause, giving heavy showers, thunder, lightning and squalls. Hail forms when strong updrafts carry frozen drops up and down repeatedly, adding layers of ice until they are too heavy.

factCards.term: Convectional rainfall: the four stages
factCards.definition: First the ground is heated strongly, warming the air above; the air expands, rises and cools adiabatically; at dew point cumulus and then cumulonimbus form; finally heavy showers, often with thunder, fall in the afternoon. Daily in the equatorial belt.

factCards.term: Relief rainfall: the stages on each side of a mountain barrier
factCards.definition: Moist sea air is forced to rise over the mountains; it cools, condenses and rains heavily on the windward slope; on the leeward side it descends, is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate, leaving a rain shadow. Ireland's western mountains get this rain.

factCards.term: Relief rainfall in India: name the mountains, wet coasts and rain shadow
factCards.definition: The Western Ghats force the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise, giving heavy rain on the Konkan and Malabar coasts, with the Deccan in rain shadow. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in the Khasi Hills, Meghalaya, are among the wettest places on earth.

factCards.term: Frontal rainfall: what happens at the warm front and the cold front
factCards.definition: At the warm front, warm, moist tropical air rises gently over cold polar air, giving long, steady rain; at the cold front the warm air is undercut, rising sharply to give short, heavy showers. This is Ireland's main source of rain.

factCards.term: World rainfall: why the equatorial belt is wet and subtropical belts dry
factCards.definition: Equatorial (0–10°): over 2,000 mm (Manaus about 2,300 mm) from low pressure, convergence at the ITCZ and convection. Subtropical high (20–30°): sinking, warming, stable air and clear skies give hot deserts, worst on west coasts beside cold currents.

factCards.term: World rainfall: the pattern in the tropics, mid-latitudes and polar regions
factCards.definition: About 10–20°: rain in summer when the ITCZ moves over, dry winters. About 40–60°: rain from depressions in the westerlies, wettest on west coasts such as Ireland's. Polar: very little, as cold air holds little vapour; Antarctica is the driest continent.

factCards.term: Cold ocean currents: effect on coastal rainfall, with two deserts
factCards.definition: Cold currents chill the air above them and make it stable, so rain is rare though fog is common: the Atacama, Chile, is the driest non-polar desert, and the Namib gets much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current. Warm currents add moisture.

factCards.term: Ireland's rainfall: key figures for east and west
factCards.definition: About 750 mm a year in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin; about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west; over 2,000 mm on many western mountains. Wet days: about 150 a year on east and south-east coasts, up to about 225 in parts of the west.

factCards.term: Ireland's rainfall: four reasons the west is wetter than the east
factCards.definition: Prevailing south-westerly winds come off the Atlantic; Atlantic depressions reach the west first; the western mountains force relief uplift; the east lies in their rain shadow.

factCards.term: Sahel: rainfall figures and why drought risk is high
factCards.definition: Roughly 200–600 mm a year, falling in one short summer wet season when the ITCZ moves north, and varying greatly from year to year. Rainfall is least reliable where totals are lowest, so drought risk is greatest there.

factCards.term: Distinctive weather regimes: four produced by ocean–atmosphere exchanges
factCards.definition: The equatorial daily cycle of morning heating and afternoon storms; the Indian monsoon's reversal of moist sea air and dry land air; fog deserts on cold-current coasts; Ireland's cool, cloudy, wet regime fed by Atlantic moisture and the North Atlantic Drift.

questions.prompt: Exchanges of water between oceans and atmosphere impact on precipitation and its distribution patterns. Discuss.
questions.model: The hydrological cycle is a closed system in which most evaporation (about 85–90%) comes from the oceans and about three-quarters of precipitation falls on them, while the atmosphere holds only about 0.001% of the earth's water and recycles it in about 9 days. Evaporation depends on temperature, dry air, wind, a large water supply, strong sunshine and low pressure, and is greatest over the subtropical oceans and warm currents. Humidity rises and falls with temperature: warm air holds about 7% more vapour for each 1 °C rise, and cooling raises relative humidity to saturation at the dew point. Condensation needs condensation nuclei, and most cloud forms by adiabatic cooling as air rises and expands, at about 10 °C per 1,000 m unsaturated and about 5–7 °C per 1,000 m once it condenses. Three types of rainfall result: convectional rain from strongly heated ground, as in the equatorial belt every day; relief rain on windward slopes, with a rain shadow on the leeward side, as on Ireland's west coast mountains and in India's Western Ghats, where Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are among the wettest places on earth; and frontal rain from depressions, with gentle ascent at the warm front and sharp ascent at the cold front, Ireland's main source of rain. World patterns follow the pressure belts: heavy equatorial rain over 2,000 mm a year where air rises at the ITCZ; wet and dry tropical seasons; the hot deserts of the subtropical highs, such as the Atacama, Chile, the driest non-polar desert; mid-latitude westerly rain, wettest on west coasts facing onshore winds; and dry polar regions, where Antarctica is the driest continent. Modifying factors include relief, distance from the sea, prevailing winds, ocean currents and the seasonal migration of the belts. Ireland's pattern shows these together: about 750 mm in the driest east around Dublin, 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west and over 2,000 mm on western mountains, with prevailing south-westerlies and the rain shadow in the east.

questions.prompt: Examine how exchanges of water between oceans and atmosphere give rise to distinctive weather and climate regimes.
questions.model: The processes come first: evaporation from warm oceans and humidity, condensation on nuclei and adiabatic cooling, and the three types of rainfall. These produce distinct regimes. The equatorial regime has moist, warm air, convection each day, morning heating and afternoon storms, with rain all year, because the ITCZ and rising air lie over the equator. The Indian monsoon reverses with the seasons: moist sea air brings a very wet summer, while dry land air gives a dry winter. Fog deserts form on the coasts of cold currents, such as the Atacama and the Namib: cold water chills the air, making it stable, so rain is rare but fog from the sea is common, and the Namib receives much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current. Ireland has a cool, cloudy, wet maritime regime, fed by moisture from the Atlantic and warmed by the North Atlantic Drift, with frontal rain from depressions, orographic rain on the western mountains and a rain shadow in the east, and wet days up to about 225 a year in parts of the west. Cold, snowy continental and lake-effect winters show how the same exchanges give snow where the air is cold and moist. Warming intensifies the cycle, increasing evaporation and bringing heavier downpours.

questions.prompt: Explain how clouds are classified, with reference to three cloud types.
questions.model: Clouds are classified by shape and by height. Luke Howard proposed the Latin names in 1803: cirrus, meaning wispy and fibrous; cumulus, meaning heaped; stratus, meaning layered; and nimbus, meaning rain-bearing. The WMO's International Cloud Atlas sets out ten main types grouped by height: high clouds above about 6,000 m, middle clouds at about 2,000–6,000 m and low clouds below about 2,000 m, with two types that develop vertically. Cirrus is a high, wispy cloud, usually bringing fair weather. Nimbostratus is a thick, dark, low cloud layer that gives long periods of steady rain or snow at warm fronts. Cumulonimbus is a towering cloud with an anvil-shaped top at the tropopause, bringing heavy showers, hail, thunder and lightning, and squalls.
